newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Commerzbank CEO sees German retail shakeout.
newsitem.headline: Commerzbank CEO sees German retail shakeout.

text.p: The chief executive of Commerzbank AG said a shake-out in Germany's retail branch business was just starting and the life of bankers will never be as easy as it was in the 1960s and 1970s.

Commerzbank's Martin Kohlhaussen said he was confident continental Europe's system of universal banks would outperform rivals because of the many financial products under one roof, which allows the banks to compensate for the temporary weakness of some activities by focusing on other areas.

"The German banking industry, particularly in domestic retail banking, is currently undergoing radical structural change, owing to insufficient earnings quality," he told bankers at the International Monetary Forum (IMC).
Banks will increasingly turn to "relationship banking" where there is a focus on highly professional core elements and therefore not offering everyone everywhere everything.
Among the reasons for the pressure on earnings was scarcity of equity capital and customer demand for more sophisticated financial products at lower prices.
Borrowers, in particular the major internationally active companies, are also turning directly to the markets.
"However, banks are not too unhappy about this development as it releases scarce equity capital for business that brings higher returns," he said.
He noted that the average interest margin of all German banks has declined since the mid-1980s and this has partly been offset by higher commisson income.
"However, the significance of extraordinary earnings, or income more dependent on market movements, has grown. So although earnings are rising, they are volatile," he said.

German banks were also facing increasing competition from non-banks, in for example private banking and Kohlhaussen said this raised the issue of supervision and whether institutions that offer the same services should be subject to the same regulation and supervision.
"Traditional branch business is on the verge of a shake-out," Kohlhaussen said.
Banks will increasingly be looking to offer off the shelf products to retail bank customers and delivering these through electronic means.
Hoewever, such new sales channels require a lot of customers for break-even and "not all the direct banks already launched in Germany will achieve this critical mass," he said.
"How earnings will be affected in the long run cannot be predicted with any certainty. But interest and commission income will probably be squeezed further," he added.
